structure.title: Act I, scene 1 · News of a battle · Which version travelled?
structure.text: The rebellion has lost Hotspur, but contradictory reports reach his father before reliable news does. Men begin making the next set of decisions while the last battle is still several different stories depending on who brought the message.

structure.title: Act I, scene 2 – Act III · Court, tavern and recruiting ground
structure.text: The king worries about succession while Falstaff encounters creditors and recruits. Justice Shallow remembers a glamorous youth. The ordinary business of supplying an army shows what nostalgia and favouritism can cost men too poor to buy their way out.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · An old king and the next one
structure.text: Negotiations in the field bring the rebels face to face with a royal prince. At home the crown lies beside a sickbed. Former friends, enemies and officers of the law must all ask what the prince will remember when the crown is his.

people.name: Henry IV and Prince Hal
people.role: A sick father and his heir
people.text: The father interprets his son's tavern life as evidence about England's future. Hal's difficulty in showing grief is sharpened by the obvious fact that the old man's death will make him king.

people.name: Falstaff
people.text: Old age, bodily complaints and persistent bills keep breaking into his performances of abundance. He treats his connection to the prince as credit that other people should be willing to advance him here and now.

people.name: The Lord Chief Justice
people.role: Officer who has enforced the law against Hal
people.text: Unlike Falstaff he has reasons to fear a personal reckoning with the incoming king. Both men must make a guess about whether personal memory or public duty will govern the new reign.

context.title: What happened in Part One
context.text: Henry took the crown from Richard II and later faced rebellion from former supporters. His son Hal fought for him against Hotspur. The battle settled the immediate danger while leaving the succession, the rebellion and Hal's tavern friendships very much alive.

notice.why: Falstaff's recruiting gives military service a wonderfully particular set of bodies and trades. The men's suitability for soldiering turns out to matter rather less than their access to cash.

notice.text: Listen to the old men finishing each other's memories.
notice.why: Shallow can turn shared youth into a claim on present friendship. Falstaff privately remembers rather different details and is quite willing to profit from the discrepancy.

opening: The king is ill, rebellion is unfinished, and Prince Hal's old companions still hope his accession will improve their fortunes. Falstaff moves through taverns and recruiting grounds, turning other people's needs into opportunities and refusing to imagine a future without his place beside the prince. Shakespeare follows the approach of a change in government through ageing bodies, unpaid bills, and friendships that mean different things to each participant. Becoming king will require Hal to decide which parts of his former life the crown can accommodate.
